content: 1. Intravenous administration of alphaprodine compared to pethidine for maternal pain management during labor was assessed in a single study. The effect estimate showed a very low certainty of evidence due to a moderate risk of bias and a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect, with few events reported. 2. Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) using pentazocine compared to PCA with pethidine was evaluated. The effect estimate was not estimable, and the certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to small sample size and few events. 3. PCA with remifentanil compared to PCA with pethidine showed a low certainty of evidence. The effect estimate indicated 19 fewer events per 1,000 participants, with a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect and a small sample size. 4. PCA with nalbuphine compared to PCA with pethidine demonstrated very low certainty of evidence. The effect estimate suggested 25 fewer events per 1,000 participants, with a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect and a small sample size. 5. PCA with fentanyl compared to PCA with pethidine was associated with low certainty of evidence. The effect estimate indicated 51 higher events per 1,000 participants, with a wide confidence interval and small sample size. 6. Intramuscular PCA with meptazinol compared to intramuscular PCA with pethidine showed very low certainty of evidence. The effect estimate was 0 fewer events per 1,000 participants, with a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect and a small sample size. 7. General relaxation techniques compared to usual care (no relaxation techniques) for pain management during labor were evaluated. The effect estimate showed very low certainty of evidence, with 1 more event per 1,000 participants and a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect. 8. Yoga techniques compared to no yoga techniques for pain management during labor were assessed. The effect estimate was not estimable, and the certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to small sample size and no events reported. 9. Music compared to usual care (no music) for pain management during labor demonstrated very low certainty of evidence. The effect estimate suggested 89 fewer events per 1,000 participants, with a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect. 10. Audio-analgesia compared to control for pain management during labor showed very low certainty of evidence. The effect estimate indicated 333 more events per 1,000 participants, with a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect and a small sample size. 11. Mindfulness training compared to no mindfulness training for pain management during labor demonstrated very low certainty of evidence. The effect estimate suggested 10 fewer events per 1,000 participants, with a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect and a small sample size. 12. Massage techniques compared to usual care (no massage) for pain management during labor showed low certainty of evidence. The effect estimate indicated 55 fewer events per 1,000 participants, with a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect. 13. Warm packs compared to usual care (no warm packs) for pain management during labor demonstrated very low certainty of evidence. The effect estimate suggested 47 lower events per 1,000 participants, with a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect and a small sample size. 14. Upright position compared to recumbent position during the second stage of labor without epidural analgesia showed low certainty of evidence. The effect estimate indicated 25 more events per 1,000 participants, with a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect. 15. Upright position compared to recumbent position during the second stage of labor with epidural analgesia demonstrated moderate certainty of evidence. The effect estimate suggested 13 fewer events per 1,000 participants, with a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect. 16. Spontaneous pushing compared to directed pushing during the second stage of labor showed very low certainty of evidence. The effect estimate indicated 17 more events per 1,000 participants, with a wide confidence interval crossing the line of no effect and a small sample size.
